stops.name: Venice, Mocenigo's disappointment and the locked attic
stops.campa: Back at San Samuele through the spring, Mocenigo grows convinced he is not being taught the secret arts he paid for and that his guest holds back the deepest doctrines; pressed by his own confessor and by disappointment curdling into suspicion, he acts. On the night of the twenty-second of May he has servants lock Bruno into an attic room of the palace, and the next day carries the first of what will become three depositions to the Inquisitor of Venice, laying out, sentence by remembered sentence, the philosopher's private table-talk on an eternal universe, a movable earth, and a Christ who worked no true miracles.

stops.name: Venice, arrest and the cells of San Domenico di Castello
stops.campa: In the night of the twenty-third to twenty-fourth of May, Captain Matteo d'Avanzo takes Bruno into custody on the Inquisitor's warrant and lodges him in the cells of the Holy Office at San Domenico di Castello. Mocenigo, not yet satisfied, brings a second denunciation on the twenty-fifth, handing over Bruno's own books seized from the palace, and a third on the twenty-ninth, now accusing him outright of reviling the Roman Church and its sacraments. The Venetian Inquisition, more temperate than Rome's, begins a methodical, almost gentle questioning that will run through the summer and autumn.

stops.name: Venice, the trial and Rome's demand for extradition
stops.campa: Through months of Venetian interrogation Bruno answers with unusual candor, admitting doubts on transubstantiation and the Trinity while insisting he is a philosopher testing truth by natural reason, not a heretic denying the faith outright; he even offers partial retraction, hoping Venice's milder tribunal will settle the matter locally. But Rome, informed of so celebrated a fugitive, formally demands his extradition, citing the still-open Neapolitan file of 1576. The Venetian Senate, however jealous of its own jurisdiction, yields in January to the Holy See's insistence, and Bruno is delivered by galley to the Roman Inquisition to answer, at last, for everything since his flight from San Domenico Maggiore.

stops.name: Rome, delivered to the Sant'Uffizio
stops.campa: Bruno is landed at Rome and lodged in the prison of the Holy Office by the Vatican, beginning what will become nearly eight unbroken years of confinement, the longest of any prisoner of the Roman Inquisition in that generation. The dossier assembled against him is now vast: the Naples file of 1576, the Venetian depositions of Mocenigo and of Bruno's own hand, and the printed evidence of a dozen books arguing an eternal, infinite, ensouled universe, a plurality of inhabited worlds, and a Christ read as a great magus rather than the unique incarnate God of the Creed.

stops.name: Rome, the commission of theologians examines the books
stops.campa: A commission of theologians, appointed to comb every surviving work for censurable propositions, spends years reducing the sprawl of Bruno's Italian dialogues and Latin poems to a list of specific heresies: the eternity of the world, the infinity of inhabited worlds, the transmigration of souls, the denial of a real distinction between the divine persons, magic and Hermetic practice mixed with natural philosophy. Bruno, examined repeatedly across these years, answers with a philosopher's patience at first, distinguishing at every turn between what he holds as demonstrated by reason and what remains, he insists, a matter of faith he does not presume to touch.

stops.name: Rome, Bellarmine's eight propositions and the refusal
stops.campa: In January the congregation approves the eight capital propositions to which the Jesuit Cardinal Roberto Bellarmine has reduced the whole case, and urges Bruno to abjure them, the last and gentlest offer of a way out the Church will make him. Bruno at first asks time to consider, and for months the case hangs in truce. But on the twenty-first of December he tells his examiners flatly that he has nothing to retract, does not know what he should retract, and does not recognize himself as a heretic at all: he is a philosopher pursuing truth, not a theologian bound by dogma he has never claimed to teach as revelation.
stops.quote: I neither ought to retract, nor will I retract; nor have I matter for which to retract.
stops.quote_source: Roman trial record, deposition of 21 December 1599

stops.name: Rome, Clement VIII orders the sentence
stops.campa: With the accused's final and formal refusal on record, the matter passes to Pope Clement VIII himself, who on the twentieth of January orders that Bruno be handed over to the secular arm as an impenitent and pertinacious heretic, the formula that seals a sentence of death by fire, since the Church may condemn a soul but will not itself shed blood. Eight years of imprisonment, examination, and negotiated silence end in this single administrative line; the philosopher who has evaded every court of Europe since 1576 has, in the end, refused the one door still open to him.

stops.name: Rome, the sentence read and 'greater fear'
stops.campa: Taken from the cells of the Sant'Uffizio and led to the palace of Cardinal Ludovico Madruzzo beside Piazza Navona, Bruno kneels before the assembled cardinal inquisitors, stripped of every clerical dignity, while the sentence of the Holy Office is read at length: heretic, relapsed, impenitent, obstinate, to be degraded and delivered to the governor of Rome for punishment as mild as possible and without shedding of blood, the Inquisition's grim euphemism for burning. Rising from his knees, Bruno turns on his judges the sentence that will outlive every one of their names.
stops.quote: Maiori forsan cum timore sententiam in me fertis quam ego accipiam.
stops.quote_source: Reported by Gaspar Schoppe, letter to Konrad Rittershausen, 17 February 1600

stops.name: Rome, Campo de' Fiori, the fire
stops.campa: At dawn on the seventeenth of February, in the year of the Church's great jubilee, Bruno is led through Rome to Campo de' Fiori with his tongue bound in a gag of wood and iron, that he preach no last heresy to the crowd, stripped, and bound to a stake atop the pyre. A crucifix is held up before his face as the flame is set; Schoppe, watching, records that Bruno thrusts the image away with a fierce look. He dies at fifty-two, having refused every court, every creed, and every offered mercy that asked him to unsay what he had seen.
stops.quote: When the image of our crucified Saviour was shown to him before his death, he thrust it away with a fierce look.
stops.quote_source: Gaspar Schoppe, letter to Konrad Rittershausen, 17 February 1600
